introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde, puis les questions 1 à 12 réparties en quatre sections de trois questions) : filigranes gcerevision.com et texte fantôme du verso (transparence du papier) ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation ni statistique précise n'est avancée ; les dates, noms, traités et lieux sont ceux de l'historiographie établie, cités de mémoire historique et à faire relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 5 : le bilan de Sharpeville (69 morts, mars 1960) est la valeur courante de l'historiographie ; les chiffres de déplacements forcés ne sont pas avancés. Les dates des lois d'apartheid et de la transition (1990-1994) sont les dates établies.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Discuss the repercussions of Apartheid in South Africa between 1948 and 1994.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Apartheid ("separateness") was the policy of racial segregation and white domination put in place by the National Party after its election victory in 1948 and defended until the early 1990s. It divided the population into racial groups (white, African, "Coloured" and Indian) and gave the white minority political and economic control. Its repercussions, meaning its results and consequences, were felt in social, political, economic and international life, and they continued after 1994.

**1. The legal framework.** The main laws included the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act (1949), the Population Registration Act (1950), the Group Areas Act (1950), the Suppression of Communism Act (1950), the Bantu Authorities Act (1951), the Reservation of Separate Amenities Act (1953), the Bantu Education Act (1953) and the pass laws. The "homeland" or Bantustan policy of 1959 and after gave nominal independence to areas such as Transkei (1976) and Bophuthatswana (1977), which the outside world refused to recognise.

**2. Social repercussions.**
- Millions of people were forcibly moved, as in the destruction of Sophiatown (1950s) and District Six in Cape Town, and families were split by the pass laws and the migrant labour system.
- Bantu Education gave Africans an inferior education designed for a lower position in society, leaving a legacy of unskilled workers and discontent.
- Poverty, overcrowding in townships and violence were widespread, and the humiliation of everyday "petty apartheid" caused bitterness and a deep racial division.

**3. Political repercussions: African resistance and state repression.**
- The African National Congress (ANC), with the Indian Congress and others, started the Defiance Campaign (1952) and adopted the Freedom Charter (1955). The Pan-Africanist Congress (PAC) broke away in 1959.
- At Sharpeville in March 1960 police shot dead 69 people in a protest against the pass laws; the ANC and PAC were banned, and the movement turned in part to armed struggle (Umkhonto we Sizwe, 1961). In 1963-64 the Rivonia trial sent Nelson Mandela and others to life imprisonment on Robben Island.
- A new generation of protest rose with the Black Consciousness movement of Steve Biko (who died in police custody in 1977) and the Soweto uprising of 16 June 1976 against the use of Afrikaans in schools. In the 1980s the United Democratic Front (1983), strikes, township revolts and the states of emergency (1985-86 and after) marked the growing crisis, and police and army violence increased.
- The system also hardened white politics, with ever more security legislation and the use of the army to defend the system.

**4. Economic repercussions.** Apartheid gave white South Africans a high standard of living on the basis of cheap African labour, but it limited the development of the economy because of the shortage of skills, a small internal market and heavy defence costs. International sanctions, the withdrawal of foreign investment and loans in the 1980s (for example the US Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act of 1986) hurt the economy and added to the pressure for change.

**5. Regional and international repercussions.**
- South Africa was criticised at the United Nations, left the Commonwealth in 1961, was excluded from many sporting and cultural events, and faced a mandatory UN arms embargo (1977).
- It supported destabilisation of neighbouring "front-line states" such as Angola and Mozambique, and held on to South West Africa (Namibia) until it reached independence in 1990. Anti-apartheid movements around the world gave support to the liberation movements.

**6. The end of apartheid.** In February 1990 President F.W. de Klerk unbanned the ANC and other organisations, and Nelson Mandela was released. After talks (CODESA from 1991) and an interim constitution, South Africa held its first non-racial election in April 1994, and Mandela became president in May 1994. The end of apartheid did not remove its legacy of inequality in land, wealth and education.

**Conclusion.** Apartheid had wide repercussions. It led to long-lasting suffering and division and to a long and costly struggle, caused international isolation and economic strain, and in the end produced the negotiated transition of 1990-1994. The inequalities it created remain a challenge for South Africa today.
